It is also said: the mawr is a movement in a swaying manner, like a thing that moves across a width, like the patella on the knee. [His saying "like the patella on the knee": it is the round bone that moves on the top of the knee, as in al-Sihah. (Ghayn)]

Meccan, and it has forty-nine verses, though it is said forty-eight. [Revealed after the surah of Sajda.]

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Al-Tur: the mountain on which Allah spoke to Musa, and it is in Madyan. "The inscribed Book, in unrolled parchment": al-raqq is a sheet. It is said: it is the skin on which the book is written, the book in which the deeds are written. Allah the Exalted said: "And We will bring forth for him on the Day of Resurrection a book which he will find laid open" (17:13). It is also said: it is what Allah wrote for Musa while he heard the scratching of the pen. It is also said: it is the Preserved Tablet. It is also said: it is the Qur'an, and it is indefinite because it is a specific book among the genus of books, like His saying: "And a soul and He who proportioned it" (91:7). "And the House frequented" (al-Bayt al-Ma'mur): al-Darih in the fourth heaven. [Its note: "His saying 'and the House frequented, al-Darih in the heaven' — in al-Sihah, al-Darih with a damma is a house in the heaven, and it is the House frequented. Narrated from Ibn Abbas. (Ghayn)."] Its being frequented is the abundance of those who visit it from among the angels. It is also said: it is the Ka'ba, because it is frequented by pilgrims, visitors and those who dwell near it. "And the raised roof": the sky. "And the sea that is filled" (al-masjur): full. It is also said: kindled, from His saying: "And when the seas are set ablaze" (81:6). It is narrated that Allah, may He be exalted, will on the Day of Resurrection make all the seas into fire, by which the fire of Hell will be kindled. It is narrated from Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, that he asked a Jew: "Where is the place of the Fire in your Book?" He said: "In the sea."

Ali said: "I do not think him other than truthful," [Al-Tabari narrated it through Dawud ibn Abi Hind from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, who said: Ali said to a man of the Jews: "Where is Hell?" He said: "The sea." He said: "I do not think him other than truthful: 'And the sea that is filled' and 'when the seas are set ablaze.'"] based on His saying: "And the sea that is filled."

Dissipation in falsehood and lies is what "al-khawd" (plunging into, engaging in) mostly denotes. From it is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And we used to plunge with those who plunged﴾, and ﴿You plunged as they plunged﴾. "Daʿʿ" means violent pushing. That is because the keepers of the Fire chain their hands to their necks, gather their forelocks to their feet, and push them into the Fire, thrusting them forcefully on their faces and shoving them in the back of their necks [[His saying "wazakhan fi aqfiyatihim" (and shoving them in the backs of their necks): in al-Sihah, "zakhahu" means he pushed him into a pit. (ʿ)]].

Zayd ibn ʿAli recited "yudaʿʿūn" (they are driven), from "duʿāʾ" (calling), meaning: it is said to them, "Come to the Fire!" and "Enter the Fire, being driven violently." It is said to them, "This is the Fire." ﴿Is this magic? Or do you not see?﴾ That is, you used to say of the revelation, "This is magic." "Is this magic?" means: is this reality also magic? The fa' (then) entered for this meaning. ﴿Or do you not see?﴾, just as you did not see in the world; that is, are you blind to what is reported, just as you were blind to the report? This is rebuke and mockery. ﴿Whether you endure it or not, it is equal﴾: "sawāʾun" is a predicate omitted, meaning: both matters are equal for you, enduring and not enduring. If you ask: why did He give as the reason for the equality of enduring and not enduring His words ﴿You are only being recompensed for what you used to do﴾?

I say: because patience has merit over impatience only for its benefit in the outcome, in that the one who endures is rewarded with good recompense. But enduring the punishment, which is the requital, with no outcome and no benefit, has no merit over impatience.

In gardens and bliss. That is, in gardens and bliss of the most perfect kind; or in gardens and bliss specifically for the God-conscious, created exclusively for them. It is also read: fākihīn, fakihīn, and fākihūn. Whoever reads it in the accusative makes it a circumstantial state (ḥāl) and makes the adverbial phrase "in gardens" stable (mustaqirr); whoever reads it in the nominative makes it a predicate and makes the adverbial phrase incidental (laghw). The meaning is: delighting in what their Lord has given them.

If you ask: what is the phrase "and their Lord guarded them" (wa-waqāhum rabbuhum) coordinated with? I say: with his words "in gardens," or with "what their Lord has given them," taking mā as a verbal-noun particle (maṣdariyya). The meaning would then be: delighting in their Lord's giving and in His protecting them from the punishment of the Blazing Fire. It is also permissible for the wāw to be circumstantial, with a qad implied after it.

It is said to them: "Eat and drink, with relish (hanī'an)," meaning: eating and drinking with relish, or food and drink that is wholesome (hanī'an), which is that in which there is no disturbance (tanghīṣ).

It may also be like the verse of the poet:

Wholesome and pleasant, free of any hidden ailment, is what has been made lawful for the honour of Izza from our reputations.

[Kuthayyir ibn Sakhr, companion of Izza, used to recite his poems in a circle at Basra. She passed by him with her husband, and he said to her: "Either you anger him, or I will strike you." She said: "Such-and-such with the mouth of the poet," and he said that. It is also said: she went out seeking ghee, Kuthayyir met her and they conversed, and he poured from a waterskin he had into her vessel until it soaked her garment. Her husband denied this, so she related the story to him, and he ordered her to revile him, and she said that. "Al-Malīk" means the master of her affair. "Mā bihā hawānī" means: she does not desire him. "Hanī'an marī'an" are two adjectives used in the manner of a verbal noun standing in for its verb, and "mā istaḥallat" is raised in position by one of them through the principle of tanāzu', while "ghayr" is in the accusative as a circumstantial state. "Min a'rāḍinā" is an explanation of what follows. "Al-hanī'" and "al-marī'" are that which has no disturbance, and whose outcome is praiseworthy. "Al-mukhāmir" is the one who mixes in. He likened her honour to a smooth drink by way of metonymy (al-makniyya). "Hanī'an marī'an" is an imaginative image (takhyīl). It is also permissible that the figurative usage in both be by way of explicit metaphor (al-taṣrīḥiyya).]

The intended meaning is a command to say: "Glory be to God and praise be to Him" at these times. It was also said that the glorification (tasbih) means prayer when he rises from his sleep, and "and at night" means the prayer of the two evenings (al-'ishā'ayn), and "the retreat of the stars" means the dawn prayer.

From the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "Whoever recites Surah al-Tur, it is a right upon God that He will grant him security from His punishment and bless him in His Garden." [Narrated by al-Tha'labi, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Wahidi with their chains of narration going back to Ubayy ibn Ka'b (may Allah be pleased with him).]

For your judgment (of their being given respite), and for the hardship and burden you will bear in it. Indeed, you are before Our eyes (فَإِنَّكَ بِأَعْيُنِنا), meaning: in a way where We see you and keep you safe.

The plural "eyes" is used because the pronoun is in the plural form of address. Do you not see His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and that you may be brought up under My eye﴾? It was also read as "wa-bi-a'yunina" (with assimilation).
